newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Mergers seen hitting Indonesia state banks' profit.
newsitem.headline: Mergers seen hitting Indonesia state banks' profit.

text.p: Proposed mergers among Indonesian state banks are seen putting a short-term squeeze on profits of banks that emerge from the consolidation, analysts said on Monday.

But they said the volatility of regional currencies, which has spilled over to the rupiah, was not expected to have a significant impact on state banks, which were seen as more secure than private banks thanks to government support.

Their prospects, however, were dimmed by reports that Moody's Investors Service was downgrading its ratings outlook on the seven state banks to uncertain from stable pending a decision on the planned mergers.
"In the short term, the merger will squeeze the profitability of the better-managed state banks like BNI," said Rajiv Louis, banking analyst with PT Schroders Indonesia.
Speculation has been rife that the government planned to merge the seven state banks into four entities.
President Suharto gave his blessing to bank mergers in late June, saying they would improve competitiveness.
BNI, the largest and only listed state bank, was likely to announce a rights issue to finance the acquisition of another bank, possibly Bank Tabungan Negara (BTN), another analyst said.
"Small investors would suffer for buying the rights as BNI's profitability is likely to be dragged down by the acquisition of BTN," the analyst said.
He said BNI's financial performance was better than BTN's, which focuses on housing loans.
Private banks, in general, have outperformed their state-owned counterparts, analysts said.
State banks are more obliged to provide liquidity credits funded by the central bank, Bank Indonesia, for certain projects, some of which are not commercially viable, they said.
The state banks affected are Bank Bumi Daya, Bank Dagang Negara, Bank Ekspor Impor Indonesia, Bank Negara Indonesia (BNI), Bank Pembangunan Indonesia, Bank Rakyat Indonesia and BTN.
They said the better-managed BNI, PT Bank Ekspor Impor Indonesia, PT Bank Dagang Negara and PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia would emerge from the consolidation.
PT Bank Tabungan Negara, PT Bank Pembangunan Indonesia and PT Bank Bumi Daya have turned in weaker performances, but analysts did not speculate on which banks would join together.

The high level of problem loans at two banks -- Bank Bumi Daya and Bank Pembangunan Indonesia -- would need to be addressed to keep them from bringing down the ratings of the banks with which they merged, Moody's said.
The Bank Financial Strength Ratings of the surviving bank or banks would depend on which institutions were combined and on the terms of mergers, Moody's said.

Moody's, however, said its existing ratings for the state banks remained unchanged and it did not expect the mergers, however implemented, to affect the debt or deposit ratings of the banks, which were based largely on their status as government banks.
The banks' ability to achieve operating efficiencies would depend on whether the government constrains or assists the banks in handling redundant personnel, Moody's said.
